html:
In 1906 Finland gave women the right to vote and to stand for parliament. It was the first country in Europe to give women the vote and the first in the world to give them full rights to both vote and be elected.

Finland was then the Grand Duchy of Finland, a self governing part of the Russian Empire. The Russian Revolution of 1905 and a general strike in Finland forced the tsar to give way. The old parliament of four estates, nobles, clergy, burghers and peasants, was replaced by a single chamber, the Eduskunta, elected by all adults, men and women alike.

At the first election, in 1907, nineteen women were elected, the first women members of a national parliament anywhere. Women's groups and the labour movement had campaigned for years.

New Zealand had given women the vote in 1893, but women there could not stand for parliament until 1919. Norway followed Finland in 1913. Finland became fully independent in 1917, after the Russian Revolution.
sum: In 1906 Finland gave women the right to vote and to stand for parliament. It was the first country in Europe to give women the vote and the first in the world to give them full rights to both vote and be elected.
